items.stem: A server has 8 workers, and each request takes 250 ms to handle. What is the most requests per second it can finish?

options.feedback: Each worker finishes 4 requests per second (1 divided by 0.25). Eight workers finish 8 × 4 = 32, which is the same as 8 divided by 0.25.
This is the rate of one worker. All 8 workers work at the same time.
This multiplies 8 by 250. A longer handler time lowers the rate, so the workers are divided by the time in seconds.

items.stem: The machine has 4 workers and each request takes 50 ms, so its maximum is 80 requests per second. The arrival rate rises to 120 per second. What happens?

options.text: Throughput rises to 120 per second and latency stays the same.
options.feedback: The workers cannot finish more than 80 requests per second, so throughput cannot reach 120.

options.text: Throughput stays near 80 per second, the queue fills and latency rises.
options.feedback: Requests arrive faster than the workers can finish them, so the extra requests wait. Once the queue is full, new requests are rejected.

options.text: Throughput drops to zero because the server is overloaded.
options.feedback: The workers keep finishing requests at their maximum rate. The users who suffer are the ones stuck waiting in the queue.

items.try: In the step "Find the maximum rate", set the arrival rate to 120 and press Play. Watch Queue depth and p95 latency.

items.stem: Requests are queueing and the machine's memory is almost full. A colleague suggests adding more workers to clear the queue. What is likely to happen?

options.text: Memory runs out and the operating system starts stopping processes.
options.feedback: Every worker needs RAM of its own. With memory almost full, new workers push the machine over its limit.

options.text: Throughput doubles, because twice as many requests are handled at once.
options.feedback: More workers only help when there is memory for them. Here memory is the limit.

options.text: The queue disappears, because the workers share the load.
options.feedback: Sharing the load does not create memory. The machine needs less memory per request or more RAM.

items.stem: A server runs at 95% utilization and still keeps up with every request. A manager says this is a good use of the hardware. What is the risk?

options.text: Waiting time is long, and a small rise in load can overload the server.
options.feedback: Above about 70% utilization, waiting time rises much faster than the load. At 95% a small increase in arrivals produces a long queue.

options.text: The workers will wear out from running at full speed all day.
options.feedback: Software workers do not wear out. The risk is waiting time and having no spare capacity.

options.text: The remaining 5% of capacity is wasted money that finance will question.
options.feedback: Some spare capacity keeps waiting time low. Running at 100% would make the queue grow without limit.
